Series::remainder¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::remainder(const Series& other) const -> Series
Series& Series::remainder_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::remainder_(const Series& rhs) const
Series& Series::remainder_(double rhs) const

What It Does¶

remainder() is the elementwise modulo of a / b that keeps the sign of the divisor b:

remainder(a, b) = a - floor(a / b) * b

floor rounds toward negative infinity, so the result always lands in the half-open interval between 0 and b ([0, b) when b > 0, (b, 0] when b < 0):

  • remainder(-5, 3) = 1 — in [0, 3)

  • remainder(5, -3) = -1 — in (-3, 0]

This is the “wrap into a range” operation: mapping an arbitrary index onto [0, n), folding an angle into [0, 2pi), or bucketing a value by a positive period. When you instead want the leftover to point the same way as the dividend, use fmod().

Parameters¶

other (const Series&)

The divisor b, which also sets the result’s sign and range. Broadcasts against the receiver.

Returns¶

Series or Series& The floored-division remainder, with the sign of b. Integer inputs stay integer. Division by 0 yields NaN (floating point). remainder_() writes the result back into the receiver.

Gradient¶

remainder() is differentiable. remainder(a, b) = a - floor(a / b) * b, and floor is locally constant, so between the jumps:

d/da remainder(a, b) = 1
d/db remainder(a, b) = -floor(a / b)

The backward passes the upstream sensitivity straight through to the dividend and routes -floor(a / b) to the divisor. Gradient does not flow through the discrete step where floor(a / b) changes.

In-Place Form¶

remainder_() is the in-place sibling of remainder(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — remainder_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({10.0, 11.0, -7.0}, {3});
auto y = pluss::make_series({3.0, 3.0, 3.0}, {3});

x.remainder_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 2]

auto x = pluss::make_series({10.0, 11.0, -7.0}, {3});
x.remainder_(3.0);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, 2]

Examples¶

Example 1. The result follows the sign of the divisor.

auto a = pluss::make_series({-5.0, 5.0, -5.0, 5.5});
auto b = pluss::make_series({3.0, -3.0, -3.0, 2.0});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.remainder(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[4], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[1.0000, -1.0000, -2.0000, 1.5000]

Every result has the same sign as its b (or is zero), unlike fmod().

Example 2. Integer inputs stay integer. This is the “wrap onto [0, n)” case.

auto a = pluss::make_series({7, -7, 7}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);
auto b = pluss::make_series({3, 3, -3}, pluss::ScalarType::Int64);

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.remainder(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2, -2]

-7 wrapped onto [0, 3) is 2, where fmod() would give -1.

Example 3. Side by side with fmod().

auto a = pluss::make_series({-5.0, 5.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({3.0, -3.0});

std::cout << "fmod      = " << a.fmod(b) << "\n";
std::cout << "remainder = " << a.remainder(b) << "\n";

Output¶

fmod      = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-2, 2]
remainder = pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, -1]

Example 4. Division by zero is NaN, not an error.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({5.0}).remainder(pluss::make_series({0.0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[nan]

Example 5. The backward passes gradient straight through to the dividend and routes -floor(a / b) to the divisor.

auto a = pluss::make_series({-5.0, 5.5, 7.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({3.0, 2.0, 4.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

a.remainder(b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity();
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity();

Output¶

da=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 1, 1]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2, -2, -1]

Each db entry is -floor(a / b): -floor(-5/3) = 2, -floor(5.5/2) = -2, -floor(7/4) = -1.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • remainder() follows the sign of b; fmod() follows the sign of a. Pick by which range you want the result in.

  • Division by 0 gives NaN; it does not throw.

  • The gradient through the dividend is 1; no gradient flows through the discrete step where floor(a / b) changes.

  • NaN in either input propagates.

Summary¶

remainder(a, b) is the floored-division modulo, signed like b:

  • a - floor(a / b) * b; result lies between 0 and b

  • broadcasts like add(); preserves integer dtype

  • NaN on divide-by-zero

  • differentiable: d/da = 1, d/db = -floor(a / b), no flow through the jumps

See Also¶

  • Series::fmod: the remainder signed like the dividend instead.

  • Series::floor: the rounding rule remainder() uses internally.

  • Series::div: the quotient this is the leftover of.
